utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. No preliminaries have been announced; so, therefore, after Mr. Registrar has called the case, the witness can be escorted in the courtroom. Yes, now let's first have the case called.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, good morning. I would just like to introduce a new lawyer on our team, Marta Bitorsoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again would like to remind that you you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. MacDonald will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist. Channel and volume. Can you hear the interpretation now, Mr. Stankovic -- still not. Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been fixed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I plan to play two more of the audio clips, and thanks to Ms. Stewart, I believe that the dialogue and the translation of the dialogue will appear from the CLSS verified translation when they are played on these occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, I'm just going to remind you of some testimony you gave on Thursday. Then I'm going to play you an audio clip of the conversation between yourself and Ratko Mladic, and then I'm going to ask you some questions. So on Thursday, at transcript page 43557, going into 43558, I said to you: "... well, genocide and war crimes are the most serious crimes. You didn't say anything to him about the severity of a potential sentence, that a life sentence must be prevented?" And you answered: "Well, you know yourself that essentially I cannot give any explanations because I don't see myself as competent, nor could I have discussed his future charges or the length of sentence because, frankly speaking, my influence on this or anyone's, when it comes to that, without the decision of a Trial Chamber, is insignificant or none. So I couldn't have discussed that in the manner that you are now presenting it." And then the Presiding Judge, His Honour Judge Orie said: "What you could have done, tell us about what you did. The question was: Did you say anything to him about -- about the potential sentence? Did you say anything in relation to that, whether you could have done it or not is -- did you or did you not?" And you answered: "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So I am going ask now for a clip to be played. For the benefit of the booths it starts on page 5 in both languages. We're looking for the words spoken by Mr. Stankovic: "Well, so then I'm afraid ..." It is going to be clip number 4 which has 65 ter number 01610e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see anything on our screen yet. There it may come. Yes, there we are. Now we still need English. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sorry, one more thing, Your Honour. I wonder if it could not be translated so Your Honours can hear the B/C/S original and then you'll see the dialogue on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we start where on the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When Professor Stankovic says the words: "Well, so then I'm afraid ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. That's the fifth box from the bottom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's impossible, I understand, to have both the text in e-court and listen to the audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm happy to say that Ms. Stewart has synced the text in Sanction, so it should simply appear, and we shan't need the e-court, Your Honours. So it should simply appear on the screen in front of you as the dialogue continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll wait and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I wonder if perhaps we could bring the transcript back up onto the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Professor Stankovic, that was you telling Ratko Mladic at the end there that "a life sentence, no matter, you see that, we have to prevent." That's you saying those words, isn't it? And before you answer ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have an objection. From the B/C/S original it was clear that this was not the end of the discussion, that it was interrupted by the second speaker. So I think to be fair to the witness we have to have the whole part listened and presented because it's all part of one spoken word. So we can't take out of context and add a punctuation point as if the sentence is completed when it's not completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything that follows, Mr. MacDonald, which might accommodate the concerns expressed by Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we turn the page in the English, Your Honours, certainly not that I'm aware of. To -- if it helps with Mr. Ivetic's objection, the Prosecution is planning to entire the entire transcript so Your Honours can see all the clips we have played in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if you're playing it for the witness, I think the witness is entitled to have the entirety of his sentence before him if you're presenting it to him out of -- out of -- pulling one piece out of context and asking him to comment as to the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, the portion played is what it is. If you think -- you have invited Mr. MacDonald to add context which you consider relevant. If is he not inclined to do, you can do so on re-examination, Mr. Ivetic. What I see is that what then follows is "we have to prevent" -- at least in the transcript it reads that Ratko Mladic then says: "Yes, yes." Whatever is there after that, you can certainly raise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, I'm just going ask you the question again. At the end of the clip we just heard, that's you telling Ratko Mladic that "a life sentence, no matter, you see that, we have to prevent."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm going to object again. He can't say "end quote" if the continuation is the next part, but that implies that it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the end of his quote, Mr. Ivetic, and if you want to add quotes later on, and you have now drawn the attention several times to the witness that he should look at what then follows. You could have done that in re-examination and that is an improper way of doing it again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, I've read you some of the words you said twice now, and that's you saying those words to Ratko Mladic back on the 9th October 1995, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one question. Will I be able to get two minutes a bit later so that I can provide my own explanation? I'm talking about the rest of my testimony. And now I will answer. So after listening to this intercept and once your examination is over, I would like to ask the Court to allow me to explain this entire position. But now I will answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you first would please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions on that clip, I would just seek to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a short question. Mr. Stankovic, last Thursday you told us that you couldn't have even spoken about the possible length of a sentence; here you do. Is that -- you're talking about a life sentence. Do you have any explanation as to the answer you give last Thursday and the answer you're giving now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to just say something. I would like to provide a general explanation. I don't want to go into details. But perhaps when the Prosecutor is done with his cross-examination, I wanted to get a couple of minutes just to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'd like to have an answer to my question. Whether -- and I'll rephrase it. Do you agree that what you told us on Thursday is not consistent with what we hear now and the answer you gave today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Just before I do, Your Honours, Professor Stankovic made reference to this as an intercept. Just to tell the Court of the origin of this tape, it comes from -- well, it was Ratko Mladic who taped this conversation and we gained custody of it when we -- well, we found it in his home, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving Professor Stankovic an opportunity to explain, a general explanation, I would like to hear in two or three sentences from him what he is going to explain. Because your main role here is to answer questions that are put to you. A opportunity will be given to clarify matters as long as it is relevant, and by one or two sentences, perhaps three, you should first introduce what you want to tell us. If that's relevant, we'll give you an opportunity. If we consider it not to be relevant, then we'll stop it there. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, I'm going play one last clip from this conversation for you. Before I do, again, I'd like to remind you of some testimony you gave on Thursday. At transcript page 43557, I said: "Now, Professor Stankovic, the indictment against Ratko Mladic for genocide and war crimes had been issued a couple of months earlier. Your meeting with Richard Goldstone, the man who has signed that indictment, issued that arrest warrant, at this meeting with Ratko Mladic, did you say anything to him like you might try to get the indictment against him withdrawn, or anything along these lines?" And you answered: "Mr. Prosecutor, I'm so small compared to an international tribunal and have so little influence or could have had such influence, that I couldn't have stated something like that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So I'd now like to play the last clip. It is 65 ter number 01610. And, again, Your Honour, thanks to Ms. Stewart -- my apologies, Your Honours, 01610f. And thanks to Ms. Stewart, the dialogue should come up on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the part that was played does not correspond to the transcript that was displayed. The additional parts were not displayed but the transcript keeps going on. So there was something unintelligible from Mr. Stankovic and then we heard General Mladic say: "No, no, let them have it," and then in the transcript it says "withdrawn." So we did not have that part of the transcript up on the recording although it was heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I saw some of "withdrawn" in the last line I looked at. So I do not know what's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We only had -- in the English on page 6, the last line shown was the third one from the bottom; whereas the audio and the conversation continues after that and we have something unintelligible and then we have Ratko Mladic disagreeing with Mr. Stankovic, saying: "No, no, let them have it withdrawn ..." I think it is very critical to what's being presented and what's being insinuated by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the text on the screen again, the text we looked at a second ago. Yes, I -- as a matter of fact, I'd like to see the text we looked at when we listened to the audio. Is it possible to that have text? So -- because that was presented when we listened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This portion we looked at, where is something missing within the confines of what we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right after the last words, Your Honour, where it says: "R Mladic: Let them have it be withdrawn ..." That is the third one up from the top in the English in the transcript in e-court. And then the conversation continues. You have Zoran Stankovic saying unintelligible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, while -- again, if there's anything in addition to what we looked at and that was played apparently if I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was played. So that's the point. It was by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's have a look at it in e-court and then we will slowly read -- we are then able to read what was for the witness presented as audio. And could you assist us, Mr. -- have it withdrawn. "Zoran Stankovic: Unintelligible. "Ratko Mladic: No, no, let them have it, and then apparently with a question mark, "withdrawn. No, no, I don't need the indictment at all." Where does it stop, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Somewhere, I think, in the middle of that last sentence that Your Honour has read, it cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So somewhere where it reads in my transcript: "No, no, I don't need the indictment" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, I think closer to the front, though, of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is what was played to the witness and what we now have looked at as transcript of the conversation. Please put your question to the witness, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, the clip we just heard, that's you speaking to Ratko Mladic again, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And when you say, "I'll try to have them deal with the indictment, you know," do you mean that you're going to try and have the indictment withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been working in this field as an expert for too long to be able to claim that any indictment could be withdrawn without a trial. So I just wanted to say the following, if you permit me a couple of minutes. At the time the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro did not recognise The Hague Tribunal. The entire material that the committee on gathering information on violations of international humanitarian law was supposed to provide to The Hague Tribunal was handed over to the United Nations in New York. During that time, representatives of Croatia and the Muslim-Croatian Federation provided their material to The Hague Tribunal. As I said, I was processing graves in Eastern Bosnia. I was processing mass graves. I worked in Siroka Kula near Gospic. No one was charged for those crimes. And then, bypassing my state, which did not want to recognise it, I came to the Tribunal on my own initiative, with a group of prisoners who had been in the war. In 1994, there was a person who was raped there. There were people who were abused, such as the priest Perkovic, and we presented this all to the Prosecutor's Office of The Hague Tribunal and we expected some sort of reaction. There was no reaction forthcoming. And so then I began to look for possibilities how to have our material reach The Hague Tribunal and how on the basis of that material people who were responsible for the death of the persons whose autopsies I carried out could be punished. So for that purpose, I was invited to London in May 1995. I went to Nora Beloff's where I spoke with a great number of people. I had a lecture in the Foreign Relations Committee in the British Parliament and also in the biggest military-strategist institute in London. Then I gave a series of lectures at other institutions in Cambridge, and I asked for help to have our documents reach The Hague. That was when people offered to defend Ratko Mladic. They said, We would defend him and also try to overturn the indictment. We would try to have that indictment withdrawn. This was something that I could not decide about by myself. I informed General Mladic about it. He recorded it as he did. It is correct that I did say what you have quoted here, and everyone knows that for genocide, if it is proved, there can be no other sentence other than a life sentence or a death sentence. So then if I used that sentence, it's possible. This is a conversation recorded by General Mladic 21 years ago. Some things -- well, I had a -- many conversations. I failed to see some things. It was not my intention to speak any untruths. But I don't see anything in particular here. I mean, everything that is stated here, I have acknowledged that I said that. Thus, my only efforts at that time were to say that the citizens and Serbs also had victims in the war. Until that time, 1995, there was no indictment issued for that, and these things were evident and everyone was aware of that. That was my only motivation, as far as General Mladic is concerned, and as far as his Defence is concerned. These people said that, We're going to get a team of lawyers together. We will appoint attorneys. We will look at the indictment. We will gather information. They said, We're a large country and we can defend even larger figures than Ratko Mladic, and we wanted to hear back from him. So I was only the messenger conveying this message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask a question, sir. Which are these people who said that they would defend Mr. Mladic? Can you name them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just say that we were in Nora Beloff's apartment. She's a well-known journalist. I didn't even know who she was when I was invited to London. I had no idea who she was. I was there, and a group of people gathered in this apartment. They discussed everything that had been going on in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and, at the same time, they wanted to engage lawyers or jurists who would defend Ratko Mladic. Not only him but other indictees as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: Who is the person who said, Yes, we will defend Ratko Mladic? What's his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot talk about names. There was just this woman I knew. There were around ten people in the apartment discussing this, but I cannot tell you their specific names because I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another question to you. Last Thursday, you were asked about a possible conversation between you and Mr. Mladic. Then you denied to have talked about these matters we are -- we have now listened to. Why didn't you explain on Thursday what you now explained today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because on Thursday, I couldn't remember all the details. And during the war and after the war, as for my activities on collecting information about war crimes and the autopsies I performed, I couldn't and I cannot remember all the details. I could not even remember where I had slept in London for ten days. I couldn't remember at all. It was just before coming here that I remembered that I had slept at the residence of the Embassy of Serbia and Montenegro in London. So that's the whole truth that I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you spoke on the phone to Mr. Mladic about your conversation with these people you are now referring to, did you at that time know the names of the people you talked to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there might be some confusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- you mentioned phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- please. Please don't interrupt me. When you had this conversation we listened to, at that time, did you know the names of these ten people in the apartment of this journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The only thing I knew was Nora Beloff. There was Marica Mate [phoen], myself, and these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you discussed these serious matters, indictment with respect to genocide, withdrawal of an indictment, presenting evidence about crimes others have committed, and you don't know the people, the names of the people? Are you telling us that story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I'm saying. Except that I know that this took place in Nora Beloff's apartment and that was even the first time that I saw her. I had never seen her before, nor had I known who she was. That was when I met her for the first time, in May 1995, in London. And that was the first time that they mentioned something like this in relation to Ratko Mladic. There were others in contacts with others, but this time I conveyed this to General Ratko Mladic when he was in Banja Luka. That was before my second visit to London, because I gave another lecture at King's College in Cambridge and I don't remember where else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you at that time know which institutions these people did represent? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I only knew what Nora Beloff told me. That's what I knew and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have a few follow-up questions here. Professor Stankovic, you're an intelligent man. On both issues - that is, talking about possible sentence and the withdrawal of the indictment - last Thursday, you did not respond directly to the questions but started explaining that you couldn't have done it, that you were not in a position to discuss these matters. Instead of giving a direct answer that "I didn't discuss it," you went beyond that, explaining what now, today, turns out to be something inexplainable. Because by telling us that you couldn't have done it, you're telling us that it did not happen. You didn't rely on your recollection, but you reasoned yourself into that answer. Do you have any explanation as to why you -- you did not tell us at that time that you just did not touch upon that matter in the conversation, why you started explaining us that you couldn't have done it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have told you that I had a great number of activities relating to war crimes in the past period that also had to do with indictment and collection of information. I couldn't remember everything at a given moment. So if that's responsibility and if that's some sort of blame, then I accept that. For some matters, time is necessary. In these three days, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are again now relying on the lack of recollection rather than to answer my question. I have one follow-up question. Did you consider discussing the withdrawal of the indictment against Mr. Mladic as a detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, a detail that we discussed while we were in this apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think you explained that you had forgotten because you might not have remembered details. Do you consider the withdrawal of an indictment against Mr. Mladic in his position a detail or would it be a major issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A withdrawal of the indictment, once it has been issued, is not possible, and I was aware of that. That it was not possible without a trial. So everything that we discussed was a trial, collecting a sufficient amount of information, to have valid information, and only after that withdrawal could take place, or a refutation of the indictment. Nothing else. It's a very difficult and complex issue. If, at that time, my position as a lieutenant colonel of the army and a specialist doctor of forensic medicine was so powerful that I could talk about a withdrawal of the indictment without a trial, then that would mean that something was wrong with me. If I was trying to resolve the issue of an indictment that had been issued in such a manner. In my explanation, I have already said, we had behind us the position of the state, which did not recognise ICTY. And my role was - and I advocated this - that as soon as the Tribunal was formed, that we should collect as much information as we could, and submit it, so that we could counter by this information what we were charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you explained to us that you considered it unfair that some were accused, where others were not accused. Had you formed an opinion at that time also about whether there were -- whether there was evidence for the charges brought against the accused, so irrespective of whether others should have been accused as well? Had you formed an opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictments that were issued against these people at the time were based on certain evidence, and the indictments have to be proven in court. So I had the information that the indictments were issued on the basis of certain evidence. Now, to prove the evidence, that was up to the court. And we were preparing to see what the evidence contained and to see what could be said in court. Just as I accepted some matters that are indisputed and that have been proven here in court, and that was our position too. The only problem was that few people were in favour of co-operation with ICTY, and willing to co-operate with it. For example, even after the fall of Srebrenica, it was said that all the documentation was taken by General Mladic, so this was discussed, and we requested that from him. We had a CD that included all the activities of Naser Oric's unit. I see now that the CD is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you a general question. Is it true that in the past, in your dealings with trials in this Tribunal, you went far, far beyond the matters on which you are called today as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depends on what I was asked. But in terms of all of the issues for which I was engaged as an expert witness, I answered all the questions as an expert witness, and I think I have done so in this trial as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not talking about what you did in this trial. I'm asking -- I was asking a general question whether, in the past, you dealt with these matters, such as preparing for the Defence, looking at whether an indictment could be withdrawn, possible sentence to be imposed, that you engaged in activities and conversations which went far beyond what your expertise in this case, and in other cases, is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question. Mr. Stankovic, were you ever charged with -- in any way with war crimes, by this Tribunal or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A minute ago, you said: "... we should collect as much information as we could so that we could counter by this information what we were charged with." Why are you saying "we were charged with"? Who is "we" in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everyone talks about individual responsibility before ICTY or any other Tribunal. If somebody commanded army, then, as the leader, he is held responsible but not just for himself, but he is also taken to account for the army that he commanded. General Mladic had 20.000 soldiers who were killed. When I invited him to surrender to ICTY, I had this on my mind. I think that these 20.000 soldiers that he commanded should be mentioned, why they died, under what circumstances, and how. Therefore, if the president of my country is indicted, the whole country is indicted. Because he did not elect himself. He was elected by the citizens, and the consequences, as can be seen, are against the country. In addition to individual responsibility, there is a general responsibility too. So when we talk about this, General Ratko Mladic is not an individual who stands accused. He is indicted together with his army, the army that he commanded. That's how I realise that. I may not be right. Therefore, that was the main point. Since the breakout of armed conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, no one is held responsible for thousands of dead JNA soldiers. I performed autopsies on them, and I requested from the state and from the state leadership to determine truth and to insist that somebody is held responsible for their death. Autopsy report was returned to me from the military court in Belgrade, and I was told: These are the victims of war. I couldn't agree with that. And all the time I have been working on collecting information so that truth would be told about those who perished. Because, as we have seen today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I stop you here. It's a lengthy answer to a short question. But that triggers a follow-up question. If I understand you correctly, every Serb soldier is accused if the commander of the army is accused of war crimes. If that is your position and you were a member of the army, is that consistent with your role as an objective expert witness in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please tell me what did I say that's not true and then you may punish me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. You -- I don't have to tell you anything. I'm asking you. Is your understanding of your role as an expert witness in this trial that you have to defend the Serb army and its commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not defend either the army or its commander. I defended the truth in which I believed on the basis of the analysis of documents. I believe that it followed from generally accepted forensic views, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One final question. You expressed your responsibility on withdrawal of indictment without trial. Did you ask anyone about whether that's possible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's the fourth time that I'm saying that I knew there was no one to ask anything. Until an indictment is issued, it's possible to withdraw it. Once it is issued, then the only instance that can withdraw it is either the one who issued it, on the basis of the trial, or if it's decided that it's unacceptable. No one else. I've said this several times now today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I said -- I think you said it's not possible to do it without a trial; but, as a matter of fact, it is. But I leave it to that because we're not here to discuss the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal with the witnesses, but since you touched upon it, I just wondered how familiar you were with the details. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours are done with questions, I'd like to correct the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At temporary transcript line -- at page 16, line 3 through 5, Judge Orie is quoted as saying: "You are again now relying on the lack of recollection rather than to answer my question." Your Honour's question was posed on the prior page, page 15, lines 18 through 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to correct me or to correct the transcript? I mean, if I said something which is inconsistent --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course, that's not a correction of the transcript, but that is an objection to how I presented matters to the witness. These two are not the same. I don't mind either of them, if you want to do it, but let's do it under right heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm try to correct the record so that we have a correct record of what the witness said, what the -- and whether it was or was not an answer to the question that was posed, because there has been an insinuation that it was not an answer to the question. And, Your Honour's question at line 18 through 21 of the prior page: "Do you have any explanation as to why you -- you did not tell us at that time that you just did not touch upon that matter in the conversation, why you started explaining us that you couldn't have done it?" And respectfully, Your Honours, lack of recollection is an answer to your question. So Your Honour's comment that it was not an answer to the question is incorrect. Later on in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked the witness something different. I think asked the witness why he did not give an answer to the question, say, That's what I did or I don't remember what I did. But why he started explaining in general terms that what we -- he was asked, whether he had done it, that he couldn't have done it rather than whether he did or did not. But let's leave it to that. It's -- I think you've made your point clear and it's on the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is your question not accurately recorded, Your Honour? Is that what Your Honour saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I think I have just one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Professor Stankovic, I'm just going to read one part of the clip we just heard and then I'm going to ask you a question. The part of the clip we just heard, it starts the fourth box in in the page in front of us. For you, Professor Stankovic, you can follow on the screen, it's at the bottom. It starts at the bottom of this page. It will go into the next page. And you stated: "Now, that is why I am going, as I said, these people, because they are very influential people ... I'm going to, when this is over, that we do away with everything we can; so that tomorrow you can move about normally, that you are not proclaimed or that they say: 'He's a war criminal' and whatnot ... we don't want to talk to him, we don't want to go like this." Now, Professor Stankovic, a couple of times now you suggested that this withdrawal of indictment may be linked to a trial, but you're not talking about a trial here back on the 9th of October, 1995. You have no idea at that point if a trial is going to happen. What you're trying to do is get the indictment for genocide and war crimes withdrawn before any trial; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Because if an indictment is issued - this is the fifth or sixth time that I am saying this - it means that it is not possible to withdraw it, especially if it's for such serious crimes, except by a decision of the court, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. I do have some documents to tender. I'm not sure if you want to do that as a preliminary after the break, possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do it as a preliminary after the break. Mr. Stankovic, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes when the re-examination will be conducted by Mr. Ivetic, and perhaps some more questions by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. With regard to the documents the Prosecution would like to tender, firstly Your Honours may remember that we tendered the photographs sent by Dr. Clark of the six bullets in the skull. Ms. Stewart has now made an excerpt of only those photographs that shown to the witness. That is 65 ter number 33753a and we simply ask that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number reserved was P7819 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now the reduced number of photographs should replace what was originally tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And I add, Your Honour, that will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will be under seal. And you're instructed to replace them. And then -- let me one second, please. One second. Yes, the P number doesn't appear on the transcript. Mr. Registrar, could you please repeat the P number that was reserved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, P7819, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second thing the Prosecution would seek to tender is the part of Professor Vincent Di Maio's book that was shown to Professor Stankovic, the page about ammunition through the ages. Ms. Stewart has again created the excerpt already. That is 65 ter 33740b. It covers -- it also includes the book cover and other pages at the start as well as the first page of the chapter, and that should be MFI'd in the meantime, Your Honours, as there is no translation as of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that there's no objection against marking for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P7820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The third document is 65 ter number 33745a, and that is the section of the autopsy report from Cancari Road 12 that was shown to Professor Stankovic, as well as photographs of the bullet and jacket from one of the wounds, as well as a fluoroscopy. Again, we'd ask that be marked for identification pending translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P7822, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 22 or 21, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I stand corrected, it's P7821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without the assistance of my colleagues I would be lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And the final document, Your Honours, is the entirety of the audio clip uploaded into e-court as under 65 ter number 01610a, and the entire transcripts in English and B/C/S are there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the length of it because we have listened only to certain portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The entire audio clip is just over 18 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is in pages, some --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It's pages 1 to 8 in the English and 1 to 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then any objections against the audio?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7822, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7822 is admitted into evidence. Professor Stankovic, sorry for dealing with some administrative matters. Mr. Ivetic will now re-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I propose to start where we have left off before the break and the audio recording of that one meeting with General Mladic that you have been discussing. My first question: Last week at transcript page 43563, you started to mention someone named Jonathan Eyal in London. Could you please tell us precisely who that person was and how they fit into what you were doing in London?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my first visit to London in May 1995, among other things, I gave a lecture about the victims of war in the largest military strategic institute in Great Britain, abbreviated as RUS. Those who greeted me there were Admiral Cobolt, Jonathan Eyal, and there were a few other people also. I gave a lecture there about these victims. Jonathan Eyal, at the time, was a man who was analysing conflicts in the area of the former Yugoslavia. He was very much quoted in our media, and I can say, judging by that, that he was a significant figure in view of the fact that he looked at what I was talking about, spoke about, victims, Serbs primarily, who were killed up until 1995 as well as the attitude towards those victims. This something that he was interested in and I described to him what I was doing. So practically he was an analyst of those conflicts and that is how he also behaved in these lectures of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I want to shift gears and focus on Nora Beloff, who you told us was a journalist and a former member of MI6, I believe. Now, last Thursday, you started to tell us about the meeting at Nora Beloff's apartment once, at transcript page 43558, and you were interrupted and not allowed to continue by the Trial Chamber. Then you also started to talk about Nora Beloff and the meeting in her apartment at transcript page 43561, and then the Prosecution interrupted you and did not let you continue. And then you again tried to talk about the meeting at Nora Beloff's apartment at transcript page 43564, and again the Trial Chamber interrupted you and did not allow you to continue with your answer. What would you have said last Thursday as to the meeting in Nora Beloff's apartment had you been allowed to continue your answer and how similar would it be -- would the continuation of that answer be to what you have told us today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a couple of things. First of all, I didn't even know who Nora Beloff was. Secondly, she invited me invited via the embassy and I received this invitation some time in early May, and that's the basis on which I went to London. When I got there, I expected a younger person but this person who was dealing with all of this was an old lady who immediately started telling me who she was and then she told me when she was born, which degrees she had. She said, I was in Russia as an agent of this intelligence agency of theirs during World War II. Well, first of all, I said that I'm not an intelligence officer. I'm such and such a person, lieutenant-colonel, and so on and so forth. So that was that conversation. Then she said, Did you bring material that speaks to the suffering of the Serbs? I said yes. And then in that conversation, the first thing was that it was said, Can we speak out, because very little was spoken about Serb victims during that period from the beginning of the war to 1995, what the truth was, and all this information, all the things that we had I brought in the form of autopsy reports. Then I gave an interview to The Times, one to the Strategic Policy, and then there was another large interview. I can't remember who for. After that, we went together to the British parliament where I gave a presentation to the Foreign Policy Committee of the British parliament, all of that. Then I went to Cambridge, and then after that, that was that first part, I talked about the problems that we had with placing the documents that we had on war crimes, that our state did not recognise The Hague Tribunal, that General Mladic did not recognise The Hague Tribunal, that the Republika Srpska leadership did not recognise it. We had problems, but the forthcoming period this would be a major problem for us, nothing would be known about our victims. And then Strategic Policy, it's a magazine that is published, its circulation is about 2.000. They talked about victims in Gospic, the things that were publicly said. At the time that is what was discussed and this is what she told me in the presence of these people, that they would like to defend General Mladic, that they would like to get the indictment, that she would like to have an interview with him, and so all of that was said. And I said, I cannot tell you anything about him. I can convey that him. He is a person who makes own decisions. He does not accept other people's opinions too much. And that was something that I did. I conveyed it. And then, again, they called me once more in September to go, and, again, I went to see General Mladic about this so that we could discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And apart from acting as a messenger to convey messages to General Mladic from this group of people in London, and potentially back, did you undertake any other efforts to assist these persons in London with their task of helping General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. You heard what General Mladic said. Already at the time he was distrustful towards everyone. He trusted just a couple of people, such as General Tolimir. I knew he was recording me. As soon as he told me, Could you please speak up, it was clear to me what he was doing. And in that entire situation, such as it was, I was just a person who was conveying. As for decisions, nobody could interview with his decision-making, least of all me. I was a messenger. I'm going to give you another example. When the Institute for War Documentation of the Netherlands wanted to speak with General Mladic and to collect data, he refused. Then they brought me envelopes for General Mladic, General Perisic, and Karadzic, and some other people. I tried to convey that and to say, These people gave me this. These were sealed envelopes. Answer the questions and I will return them. He said, Take it back. Who told you that you could take that? And I took it back, and I still have it to this day. The envelope is still sitting at my house with its seal intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for sake of clarity, you indicated the Institute for War Documentation of the Netherlands that would be known under the acronym NIOD?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now moving to a slightly different but related topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do so, I have one question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just told us about your conversation and prevention at the Foreign Policy Committee of the British parliament, and I would like to know on whose behalf you told them, "that our state did not recognise the Tribunal, that General Mladic did not recognise it, and that the Republika Srpska did not recognise it"? They're your words you just told us. On whose behalf did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my own behalf. Because that was true. As I said in 1994, I was in The Hague with a group of camp inmates, and there was talk about us directly co-operating with The Hague Tribunal because that was the court that was formed. I think Dusan Tadic was already in prison. I visited him on that occasion. I said, That court will pass -- hand down judgements. You must co-operate with them, otherwise the state will just have negative results and negative connotations if it does not do that. So, actually, that was my own personal position on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated last week, I believe, that you had contacts with Carla Del Ponte and others from the Prosecutor's office of the Tribunal. Were any of those contacts to render assistance to General Mladic, or were they to assist the work of the Prosecutor's office of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It's quite a leading question, Your Honours. I wonder if it might be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the contacts that you had with Carla Del Ponte and the members of the Prosecutor's office of the Tribunal that you told us about last week, were any of those meetings in relation to assisting General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Still leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the contacts that you had with Carla Del Ponte and the members of the Prosecutor's office of the Tribunal that you told us about last week, what were the topics or themes that were discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents collected by the committee for gathering data on violations of international humanitarian law of the Government of Serbia and Montenegro were discussed. Also, implementing the obligations of the state vis-à-vis The Hague Tribunal. That was discussed. About the arrests of people who had indictments issued against them. This is something that was discussed within the committee for gathering information, and I was only present as a member of the committee. Professor Dr. Zoran Stojanovic, professor of criminal law at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade, who was also the federal minister of justice at the time, was the chairman of that committee. So I was just present at the meeting. I asked, what about evidence that we furnished that had to do with victims in these locations, and when indictments would be issued against those people who were responsible for the deaths of people whose autopsies I carried out. They didn't promise or offer anything to Ratko Mladic. No offers of help of any kind were given. The discussion dealt strictly with adhering to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I want to move to a different topic, and that is your engagement in this case that we are here for today. Could you tell us how and when you were engaged by the Defence for serving as an expert in this case.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in late 2014 and early 2015 when the Defence offered me the opportunity to be an expert witness dealing with the mass grave in Tomasica, and I accepted that, and I wrote and submitted the report that I wrote and submitted. After that, in October of last year, after Professor Dunjic died, the Defence again asked if I would accept to speak and to present in a certain way Professor Dunjic's report before The Hague Tribunal's Trial Chamber, in view of the fact that in an earlier period I did an expertise on 2.082 mortal remains in the case of General Krstic. I agreed, and that is how I ended up being an expert witness in these two cases -- in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point time seek out the Defence prior to that time to seek to be an expert at this trial?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never offer my services to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecution stated at transcript page 43554 that you have a "close personal relationship" with General Mladic. When you attempted to answer that question, they cut you off and did not let you answer that question. Do you consider that you have a close personal relationship as a friend of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I know that some conversations that I had with General Mladic were recorded by him, but I can say that as far as he is concerned and people like him who lost close family, their children, and whose autopsies I performed, I was ready 24 hours a day to respond to any call from them, to speak with them, about autopsy details or whatever they wished to talk to me about. Therefore, I kept saying -- I kept talking about that special relationship that we have. General Mladic never behaved as a superior officer towards me. He constantly viewed me as the person who performed the autopsy of his daughter and that is how he behaved. He behaved like that. Also, when he was placing his daughter in the coffin, when he placed the makeup on her, this is how he behaved whenever we were in contact. And that is that special relationship that perhaps people cannot or do not want to understand. I pray to God, even though I'm not a religious person, never to have -- never to form friendships in the same way that my friendship with Ratko Mladic was formed, because of the death of his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated in your answer that -- for people like him who lost close family, their children, and whose autopsies you performed, you were -- you are ready 24 hours a day to respond to any call. In how many cases have you had personal interactions with persons who are family members of -- of persons upon whom you performed an autopsy as a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made a calculation. Out of 5.000 autopsies of children who were victims during war and that were conducted at the forensic medicine institute of the VMA in Belgrade, we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we get a translation of what Mr. Ivetic has just said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He said: The interpreting service is not able to follow you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, could you please start your answer from the beginning and try to speak slower so that the translators can follow you and we can get the entirety of your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forensic medicine institute of the military medical academy during the war performed autopsies of 5.000 persons who were killed in the war-torn areas. Each of those bodies were shown to members of the family in view of the fact that all of them or some members of the closest family wanted to see the mortal remains. We estimate that at least four people during these viewings -- would attend these viewings and we would show the mortal remains, and this amounts, in the seven or eight years that we did that, to about 20.000 family members with whom we were in contact when we were showing the mortal remains of their close ones to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't think the last part of the answer was translated. At least I heard something in B/C/S and I heard nothing in English afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask the witness to repeat himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I -- Witness, Mr. Ivetic says that some of what you said was not interpreted. I'll read to you what at this moment we see on our transcript, and please add whatever you may have said in addition to that. The last we read is: "... in the seven or eight years that we did that, to about 20.000 family members with whom we were in contact when we were showing the mortal remains of their close ones to them." What did you say after that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing more than that. It's all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, have your interactions with Mr. Mladic, including this one meeting 20-odd years ago, had any effect upon your ability to review the autopsy reports that you reviewed in this case in an objective manner?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My mother, who was an orphan of war and whose father was killed in the World War II, told me when I completed my studies, she said, I suffered a lot, I am from a family of workers and peasants, and it was difficult for me to complete your education. Please never say something that is untrue in your work. Don't add or subtract anything for anyone. I was the best student at school, but after my father's death, I remained in the country and I had to work the fields and I had a hard life. For me this is the greatest obligation and I'm trying to fulfil it to this day with regard to anyone and everyone and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to return to your actual evidence as an expert witness. You have seen now from cross-examination because you were shown a photograph from Dr. Clark and the autopsies that were not provided to be reviewed as part of the autopsy records. How does this compare with the usual practice as to photographs taken during autopsies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. I would object to that question as confusing, Your Honours. Mr. Ivetic introduced the idea that it wasn't reviewed as part of the records and then asks about, from what I can see, taking photographs during autopsies. So I'm not sure which procedure he is actually asking Professor Stankovic to comment upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is unclear to Mr. MacDonald, perhaps, Mr. Ivetic, you could phrase the question in such a way that he even understands it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try to break it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a photograph said to be taken by Dr. Clark in relation to the six bullets to the head of a particular Tomasica victim. First of all, was that photograph included in any of the autopsy materials that you reviewed from the Tomasica file?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have photographs while reviewing these autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The explanation given by the Prosecutor last week was that Dr. Clark had just given them those photographs. How does that compare with the usual procedure of photographs taken during autopsies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the autopsy report is completed, so should be the photographs, and a photo file is compiled as an additional part of the autopsy report. It should be relating to the specific case, Tomasica 37-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would photographs as part of an autopsy report assist a pathologist, such as yourself, such as Dr. Dunjic, or anyone else, to be able to review and understand those autopsy records better?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially as photographs from this autopsy were really well taken. They're high-quality photographs, and one may discern in them everything that was done during the autopsy and where the projectiles were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is everything depicted in the photographs identified in the written autopsy report description for the injury wound -- for the injury report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though I requested the Bosnian-Herzegovinian autopsy report, I did not find it among the reports that were submitted, but Dr. Clark described it in several sentences on page -- on one page of his summary report. He says that six projectiles were found in the skull, and he mentioned the exact locations where those projectiles were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the cross-examination at transcript page 43545, you were asked about your previous testimony in the Krstic case in relation to blindfolds at the Srebrenica grave-sites. To refresh your recollection, these are the 367 cases you could reasonably assume were executions, saying those were those including ones -- pardon me. Were those 367 cases including cases where there was only a strip of cloth around the eyes or did they all have ligatures around the hands or legs, if you remember? Do you remember the numbers of each?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that piece of information in the Seselj trial. My finding which has more details was presented in the Krstic case. These were blindfolds, ligatures on the arms and the legs, taken all together, not separately. I don't know how many blindfolds and ligatures on hands and legs there were separately or all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your use of the term "blindfold," can you explain for us forensically the evidence you would like at to differentiate between an actual blindfold, on the one hand, and a strip of cloth that had been tied around the forehead as a bandana that had potentially slipped down post-mortem?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I looked at was primarily the description of the blindfold in the autopsy report, whether it extends over the eyelids, is it above the ear lobes or not, or across the ear lobes or below the ear lobes, considering the possibility that blindfolds located above the ear lobes could have been tied across the forehead and may have slipped down, depending on the position of the body in the grave, as we have said, due to the loss of soft tissue in the areas where they were tied and so on and so forth. So primarily, we focused on where and how those blindfolds were tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could have look at D1448 MFI in e-court, this should be Dr. Dunjic's report that you provided testimony about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And once we have that document, if we could turn to page 70 in the English and page 65 in the Serbian, and I believe it will be at the bottom of the page in both languages. We're still waiting for the, I think, Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this section of Dr. Dunjic's report, he is talking about the reporting of Prosecution witnesses. And we see here that as to some of the alleged blindfolds that were recovered by the Prosecution in Srebrenica, these alleged blindfolds are actually recovered loose in the grave rather than being affixed to any bodies? Forensically speaking, to a degree of medical certainty as a pathologist or court forensic expert, can we exclude these blindfolds found looses in the grave, not affixed to bodies, from being strips of cloth that were previously worn as bandanas and slipped off the foreheads of bodies?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several possibilities. First, that the blindfolds slipped from someone's head during the burial. Second, that they may have been on the clothes or somewhere else, not on the head. So these are two main possible causes as to why there are some separate blindfolds in the mass grave. They may have slipped from somebody's head or they may have been on some other part of the clothes and were then found in the mass grave loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the bodies exhumed from graves in Srebrenica, where the strip of cloth goes above the ear, can one with certainty exclude the possibility that these strips of cloth worn bandana-style over the forehead?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That possibility cannot be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Moving on. You were asked in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you changing subject or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, changing subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask, when you prepared this report which was presented in the Krstic case about the 367, did you -- at that time, had you considered also whether what you then described as blindfolds could be bandanas which has -- had slipped down, or had you considered that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did not take that possibility into account at the time. It was only when I saw the position of Professor Dunjic that I took this possibility into account and I could not exclude it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it never came to your mind when you drafted the report in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation as to why you didn't think about that and now, in relation to Dr. Dunjic, his report, that you say you can't exclude it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I simply did not see this possibility. I was not aware of it when I testified. And after having seen Professor Dunjic's report which he envisaged, I could not exclude it any longer. And at the time when I testified as an expert witness, I simply never considered this possibility or whether they wore those bandanas across their forehead or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Saying that you can't exclude it. Did you form an opinion about the probability also in relation to the position of the bodily remains in the mass graves? I mean, just for record --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think I asked whether you formed an opinion about the probability of that also in view of the position of the bodily remains in the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you first asked me here what is the position of bodies in a grave, whether they are horizontal or vertical, lying or standing, and I then said that if they were in one of the upright positions, a sitting position or so, then it's possible for such a bandana to slip down. But not necessarily. So I cannot speak with any certainty whether they slipped down or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the body is horizontal, then you wouldn't consider it a possibility, an option, that the bandanas would have slipped down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The likelihood would be very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for Your Honours as well, Dr. Lawrence on 19th of July, 2013, also talked about the -- of being unable to exclude the possibility of a strip across the forehead falling down across the eyes as the body began to fall part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's argument, but you're referring us to relevant portions of the evidence, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution does it every time, so I think I'm entitled as well to point to evidence that is [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that is true, neither of you are entitled, let it be clear, even if I said that it's okay at this moment. So I would have accepted that if I were you, but, of course ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during the cross-examination, you were asked about a wound whose scar tissue was shown to you in a photograph and that was at transcript page 43509. And my question for you, sir, is how does -- how -- the -- in terms of diagnosing the cause of a wound, is it better to have access to the scar tissue or to the fresh wound? Medically speaking, which is easier to diagnose?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly easier to make a diagnosis if you are dealing with a fresh wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at transcript page 43518 to -19, you were asked as follows, beginning at line 21 of that day's transcript. The question posed to you was as follows: "Q. Professor Stankovic, with regard to the criticism of Professor Dunjic of Dr. Clark that he makes an assumption regarding the injuries found on the bodies, that assumption being that the wounds were inflicted in life. If the forensic pathologists who did the thousands of autopsies on bodies and bones from Srebrenica, if each of them had said in their cause of death section, If these wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death, would that resolve the -- that particular criticism of Professor Dunjic?" And your answer was: "I think that it would, yes." And my question for you is a bit different. Would this, as suggested by the Prosecutor, the addition of these words in the pathology reports, would that have resolved the complaints and objections raised by both you and Dr. Dunjic as to the lack of descriptive detail in the trauma or injury section of autopsy reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would the addition of words suggested by the Prosecution have resolved the complaint and objection that both you and Dr. Dunjic raised as to conclusions by Prosecution pathologists that certain injuries were homicide or undertaken with a specific intent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not understood your question sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would -- let me rephrase it this way. Would adding the words "if these wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death," would that have resolved the complaints and objections that you voiced and that Dr. Dunjic voiced that certain Prosecution pathologists were rendering opinions that the death was a homicide or that the injuries were inflicted with a particular intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no problem with my friend's question up until the last words. We certainly agree that some of the autopsy reports recorded homicide, but, as far as I am aware, they do not say homicidal intent. And I'm unaware of any pathologist concluding upon intent. My friend may be thinking about one of the pathologists talking about post-mortem injuries, but that is a separate issue that Dr. Dunjic raises. It's not to do with the autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there's a suggestion that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm about to actually read that section. If I could just have a moment to find it in my notes from last week. I believe we had -- here it is. We had in Dr. Dunjic's report, at page 26 in the English and in the Serbian it was page 25 at the bottom, a question relating to the results as to Cancari 3 and CR-12, document 00920598 to 652 in relation to C.H. Lawrence. Since I cross-examined him, I'm pretty sure he was a forensic pathologist who was a Prosecution expert witness, but I could be wrong. And in summary, the conclusions from this cite C.H. Lawrence noted under item 12: There were many post-mortem tampering injuries of the skull, ribs, and pelvis which would tend to obscure perimortem injuries in these regions. So that in sense, the pathologist is definitely talking about the injuries being with an intent to obscure perimortem injury and that was a topic that Professor Stankovic testified about last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it tend or intent? I think that's what keeps you apart which -- a certain situation may tend to -- to -- as it's said here, to obscure, not necessarily intentionally obscure, but which is of a kind that could obscure other injuries which were inflicted at an earlier stage. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I might add to this discussion some information, Your Honours. This was raised with Dr. Dunjic in Karadzic testimony and it transpired that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, let's -- the -- you have an opportunity to do that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: But it's about a translation question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a translation question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. It transpired that the B/C/S that Dr. Dunjic reported had the word "intentional" in it, which did not appear in the original English. That came up in Dr. Dunjic's Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if that assists you in -- at least in the English text that there's no intent mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've read the English, of course, so I -- I don't have the B/C/S in front of me to make a comparison but I would be happy to do so. And if that's the case, let me rephrase the question a third time to try to avoid that confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do, what does the English say, does it say "tend" or "intent," the one that you are reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have to go back and find it. I have been flipping through the pages, but I believe I read it -- the English that I read is the -- is the English of Dr. Dunjic's report, so if there is an issue of the translation, we would have to look at Dr. Lawrence's report, which I don't have in front of me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, if the word "tend" would have been written as "intent," the whole sentence becomes rather difficult for me to understand. But if you would verify it, that would be appreciated. But then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could limit then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I apologise. If we could limit, then, my question to the aspect of homicide, would simply adding that "if the wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death," would that affect or change your objections to certain pathologists determining that injuries were the result of homicide?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we talked about. If the injuries were sustained in life, if as a consequence of these injuries - for example, the destruction of the bones of the skull - we can say if it's a gun-shot injury to the head inflicted in life, then the cause of death is the destruction and the damage of life-giving centres in the brain, then the cause of death is this gun-shot injury to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I feel we are having a translation -- we're missing each other in the translation. Since I'm talking about homicide and ... let me try it this way. Would adding the words "if these wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death," without changing any of the other findings in the autopsy report, would that affect your complaints and objections to certain pathologists making conclusions of homicide or, in the B/C/S, "ubistvo"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say what is the origin of death, whether it was homicide or suicide or accidental, if that's what you have in mind, then, in principle, on the basis of all the arguments, it's the Trial Chamber that decides what was the origin of death.
