At the moment when there is a single gun-shot injury to the head, it may have been inflicted in combat or it may have been execution, intentionally inflicted by another person, that is to say, or it may have been the consequence of suicide or the consequence of an accident. We've had that in the army. If a soldier is cleaning a weapon, then it fires, and then an accident occurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask, is there any dispute about this matter, apart from, of course, the legal connotation of homicide not being the same in every system, but that if you find a dead body with an injury which would -- without any doubt, such as a gun-shot wound in the head, would -- certainly there's a possibility that it would have been inflicted by someone who executed or intentionally killed, but that it's not for a forensic pathologist to decide whether that was the case or whether it may have been an accident, is there any dispute about this? Because that's what you are apparently bringing to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If there is no dispute, then I'm quite happy. But the Prosecution has presented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- evidence of their own Prosecution expert saying that it is, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first ask whether there's any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the -- well, from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Carefully read what I said and tell me whether there's any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: We certainly agree that when it comes to whether or not someone has been executed, intentionally killed, are really the question of intent and that's for the Trial Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if it would have been an accident, then you might see exactly the same on the body and the person may have died from that gun-shot injury, but it's not necessarily homicide -- it's -- it's -- it -- it may be accidental rather than intentional. That's a possibility. I'm just wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there is a slight difference here in that we understand it is a cultural matter that pathologists, particularly from United States, use "homicide" simply to say the killing of one person by another person without reflection upon intent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the other matter I raised, which is that "homicide" is not an unambiguous expression in legal terms, depending on the system we're working in. I think we have explored this with sufficient detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's time for a break. I would like to know how much time would you still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would think six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six minutes. That's the type of accurate assessment I like very much. Mr. Stankovic, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes for another six minutes of re-examination. And how many minutes for you, Mr. MacDonald, as matters stand now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm currently between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm currently between zero and one question, Your Honour. I'm just trying to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm more interested in minutes than in questions, but -- please, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, Exhibit P7819 was admitted under seal. However, upon verification with the -- verification by the Registry with the Prosecution, there is no need to have it under seal. Therefore, P7819, which are the photos of the bullets to the head, is a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I do understand that you need until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, one last question in relation to the topic we were talking about before the break. You testified several times, and in relation to Dr. Dunjic's report, about the failure of the Prosecution forensic experts to adhere to the classical method of what they note in the autopsies and saying that it -- they often only had summary findings that then could not be verified by another expert. Would that objection or complaint still remain even if the Prosecution experts added words to the effect that if these wounds were inflicted in life, then they were the direct cause of death; that is to say, would the addition of those words affect your complaint as to the failure to adhere to the classical method?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We stated our objection. It is our position that all injuries should be described in detail. As I repeated several times, the place needs to be located, the description given. Everything that has to do with an injury would need to be stated and put into the autopsy report. We believe that only a descriptive diagnosis would be a professional insufficiency, a failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you were shown document 33693 during cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask for that same document to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think it was page 3 of the same that you were asked about. This is the autopsy protocol of (redacted) that you yourself were involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be broadcasted in its unredacted form.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I apologise. Then if we could not broadcast the same. Do we then need a redaction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was not primarily the name but it was, rather, the details, the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if the Prosecution disagrees, then I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I agree with your assessment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, now we have the document before us. First of all, Doctor, are you asserting a cause of death anywhere in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only with a certain degree of probability. Because I repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please indicate where he is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive interpretation. And when you are reading from the document, please indicate where you are reading from. That would help the interpreters. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that we can see on the screen, page 3, the section, opinion, item I: "The body of a male exhumed from the soil in a skeletonized state. The autopsy alone cannot establish with certainty the actual cause of death."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And last week we already talked about the correct translation of the fifth item under your opinion as to what degree of probability you were assigning. Can you identify for us the various levels of probability that are used in forensic work of a pathologist and where on this scale these findings would lay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, there are three degrees of probability, or, rather, three degrees that we use in forensic medicine. Definite is one of them, where the answer implies that there are no dilemmas; most probably, where it is indicated that the opinion is most probably correct but not 100 per cent certain; and then reasonably. It can reasonably be assumed where an assumption can be made but it does not have to be that necessarily. In short, that is the lowest possible degree of probability, meaning that there are reasonable grounds to assume something, and that would be the lowest degree of certainty or probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now my last question is on another topic. At transcript page 43543, you were asked about Dr. Haglund's revised story about the role of Prosecutor Peter McCloskey in the collection of autopsy records and the examinations of the San Antonio Oversight Committee, and the question that was posed to was as follows: "Q. You'll know that Dr. Haglund said at transcript page 14920 to 14921: 'That's -- that's -- that's what they questioned, and actually Mr. McCloskey took the -- all of the writings on how -- what the -- what the pathologists had done and he went all over the world, and -- to see if they needed to have their -- their writings changed or if they were -- if it was the same way it was, and then they would change it, and then he would go on to another country and find another people. So he went basically all to the -- I think there were 30, 30-some pathologists that we had from Turkey, England, United States and all over. And that's -- he carried things around, but Mr. McCloskey, of course, didn't change anything. It was none of his business. He just took it to the pathologists.'" And now the question I want to ask of you, Professor, from the standpoint of a forensic science expert and forensic pathologist, how do you consider these activities in the revised account of Dr. Haglund, are they in accord with the generally accepted practice relating to autopsies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm just wondering of my friend's use of the "revised." Revised story, revised account. So far -- as far as I am aware -- I'm not sure if my friend is implying that Dr. Haglund once said one thing and now says something else. If he could just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In presenting this to the witness in cross-examination, the Prosecution was relying upon what had been taken from Haglund's previous testimony and was in the Dunjic report, and they were saying that Haglund had explained that in a different way, with more details, subsequent to that and they were asking that of this witness. And so it is a revised account. It is a subsequent account that gives more details than what was cited in the Dunjic report as to these matters - I'm trying to find the page number of the same right now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether or not subsequent or revised, let's focus on what he says here. And you are, I think, asking about how -- whether it's appropriate to do it this way and you're focusing on this account.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And I can give you the 65 ter number of the prior account where he has a different description and that is P1831 in our case, English page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's focus on what you want to hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you've heard what Mr. Haglund said that Prosecutor McCloskey was involved in. From the standpoint of a forensic pathologist and expert in forensic science, how do you consider these activities? Are they in accord with the generally accepted practice in the field as you know it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would be realistic to expect that if somebody wanted to verify somebody's findings, they would request that in writing and would also submit the entire material to the expert they were engaging, with specific questions, requesting specific answers to the things that they were interested in. It is not customary for a member of the Prosecution, or anyone else from the investigation side, carries documents around without having a written order as to what somebody was supposed to say about a specific document. And it's not customary for what is written then is not then in the documents that are being discussed today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, I thank you for answering my questions. I have no further questions for you. And thank you for your patience. I know we went longer than anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Well, six minutes became 12, but, still, a very limited number of minutes. Now you, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Professor Stankovic, this concludes -- if my colleagues have no further questions and I don't have any further questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having stayed with us for quite a while and having answered all the questions, whether put to you by the parties or by the Bench. You may follow the usher, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just say a couple of sentences. I thank you for the specific questions, to the professional attitude of the Trial Chamber towards me, and I wish you all the luck in your further work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution -- is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope we are, Your Honours. They should be in the back. I haven't heard anything other than that. But Professor Radovanovic would be our next witness and I am prepared to question her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, I should have asked the usher to bring her in right away, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if Ms. Bitorsoli, Mr. McCloskey, and I might be excused for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Radovanovic. Before you give evidence, even if it's renewed evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. No need to say that he's to your left. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we may perhaps have the microphone adjusted downwards. I suspect we night have some issues from the booth if it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Professor. It's good to see you again.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since we have last time gone through your background, your career, and your CV, I will not do so again today, but I would ask that you please state your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Svetlana Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could tell us, Professor, were you tasked by the Defence team in relation to the Tomasica evidence?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And before we get to the terms of that tasking, I would like to take a look in e-court at 65 ter number 1D06184, of which I have a hard copy to be given to the witness to assist her in going through the same. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And my first question, Professor: Do you recognise this document that you now have in hard copy and which we have on our screens before us?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report that I wrote after looking at the report and other materials used by the Prosecution expert, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone other than yourself take part in the drafting of this report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by the report as written or are there any typographical errors or other errors that you wish to correct with us today?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do want to correct some errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could first turn to page 17 in the Serbian and page 13 in the English, and I would like to focus on footnote number 26 of the same. And in relation to footnote number 26, what would you like to draw to our attention or correct here?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This footnote, footnote 26, should say "See footnote 24."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we can look at page 20 in the Serbian and it will be page 16 in the English, and paragraph number 42 of the report. And if you could take a look at that and tell us -- actually, we should wait for the -- okay, now we have it in both languages. Professor, if you could look at paragraph 42 and tell what us you would like to say about this paragraph and any corrections necessary.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This paragraph should be omitted because yesterday I established that the quote that I cite here, the quotation of Dr. Tabeau, does not correspond to the English because the translation actually is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say the translation is different, are you referring to the Serbian translation that was provided of Dr. Tabeau's report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received an official or a certified copy of Dr. Tabeau's report, and this translation does not correspond to the report that is written in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from striking it from this report, could I invite the Prosecution to present a new translation because it's a B/C/S translation and apparently there's a translation error. If it's there, the existing one should be replaced by the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is a slight error. I don't know if we can deal with it in court. It's basically that "DNA" has been inserted in the Serbian where there is no "DNA" if we're matching in the English. So it's -- it's a small error that could perhaps be dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it explains a wrong paragraph in the new report, then there must be -- there must be really a difference between the two. Otherwise -- so therefore I would like to have it verified exactly what now the proper translation in B/C/S would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We're happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, apart from these corrections which we have now gone through in the courtroom today, do you feel that you need to make any other corrections to your report or do you stand by the same as having been correctly written?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it is fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to turn to page 3 in both versions of the report. And here in the report you have a listing of reports and data sources studied and analysed. Could you confirm for us if you used any sources outside of what is -- strike that. Could you confirm for us what sources you had at your disposal for purposes of preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cited them here. I can read them out one by one. Otherwise, I agree with what is stated here under numbers from 1 to 90 [as interpreted], with the observation that from the 11th to the 17th of January, I was here at this Tribunal, and I asked to look at specific documents so that I could review them. The Defence submitted this request to the Prosecution in a timely manner as to which materials I wanted to look at, and I refer here about the documents that I received that I wished to look at and also those that I requested but did not receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you say numbers 1 to 90 or 1 to 19?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in both versions. And I think here we'll see the part that you just told us about, and you say you were not given all of the requested material for your inspection. Could you detail for us what was the most significant of the material which you did not receive for purposes of your inspection that had been sought from the Prosecution as identified in this last paragraph of the page.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not receive the Red Cross material from 2005. I did not receive certificates of death. And I did not receive the criteria on the basis of which Dr. Tabeau did the matching. I would also like to note that before I appear in court, I'm asked to submit my request about the materials that I wanted to review. I submitted a request, and the request contained all the material that I wanted to look at, including some materials that I did receive, but also the request included material that I did not receive, and I did not get any explanation why this material was not given to me for my review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, did you immediately report that you did not receive materials you had asked for to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told the Defence that I did not receive certain materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you assist me, my recollection doesn't serve me well, Mr. Ivetic. Has this been brought to the attention of the Chamber and has the matter been raised in court or by other means so that we could have repaired what may have been wrong since January?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By other means, Your Honours. We met with the Prosecutor in relation to the request. In relation to the certificates of death we were told that they had disclosed to us everything that they had received from the BiH prosecutor's office and that that was what it was, that they didn't have any additional certificates of death. Then Your Honours might recall when Madam Tabeau testified back in -- last year, as to Tomasica, we asked her in court for the matching criteria that were utilised by her for Tomasica and Madam Tabeau said that would take time. Your Honours said that obviously she did not have to do it that day, and since that date we have not received criteria from the Prosecution demography expert, the matching criteria that they used for Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you addressed either the Prosecution or this Chamber to ensure that what you needed or what your expert needed would be provided even if that could not be provided within one day?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it was my understanding that when Ms. Tabeau was in court she promised she would do the criteria, and that was in relation not only to my request but Your Honours' request, and so I -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then you wait until the end of April to establish that it's not there or -- I mean, if it is it important --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We had meetings with the Prosecutor and that was the -- the matching criteria was item number 13 on our list that was given to the Office of the Prosecutor, of which I had at least two meetings with Mr. Traldi and Ms. D'Ascoli in relation to the same and I -- you know, if the criteria --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's without --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- aren't ready, they're not ready. I can't -- I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's without result, then the usual way of proceeding is to ask the assistance of the Chamber. Because this Chamber has one thing clearly on its mind. Whatever we can do to assist the parties that they receive the material they need, we'll do it. And now we find ourselves, late April, in a situation where it's not there. And that it was all unexplained, to some extent, if I understand it well, it was explained, although perhaps that explanation may not have reached the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you referred to the meetings with Mr. Traldi. When did they take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There were several meetings, Your Honours, that were before the trip of the experts in January. The original list was presented, I believe, by, as I recall, Mr. Lukic in a meeting he had with members of the Prosecution even before the meeting was scheduled so it was -- that would have been late 2015. And, of course, the meeting -- pardon me, the trip of the expert to The Hague occurred in January of 2016 as they have listed there. I have one additional matter to raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic I just wanted to know, you referred to testimony number 123 on a list given to the Office of the Prosecutor. When was this list given to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Item 13, Your Honours, on the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay, that's correction --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- so that's a correction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a correction for the record. When was that given to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It would have been, I believe, sometime in November of 2015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And once it was established in January that not all the materials were available that the expert witness needed, were there other meetings to try to resolve that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Because Madam Tabeau testified when she testified as to Tomasica that she did not have those. She would have to create them. And so my understanding of the rules, as Your Honours reminded me last week, when something is not in the possession of the Prosecution, I can't ask for them to be enforced to disclose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So until it is completed by Madam Tabeau, I have nothing to ask for. I can only note that we haven't received it. And then I ask the expert what that means in terms of the work of a demographer and how such criteria are utilised, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think we are mixing up two things. First of all, what should be disclosed, there is no need to disclose anything which is not in your possession. That's a different matter from asking what you may need. And I'm a bit confused because a minute ago you told us that you understood that Ms. Tabeau would on the instruction of the Chamber produce something, and then you said you met, although not after January when it became clear that that material was not there, you met with the Prosecution. Where I would have expected that, to the extent your understanding is correct, and let's just assume that for argument's sake, that then you would have addressed the Chamber and would have asked the Chamber to urge Ms. Tabeau to produce what you say she was instructed to produce. I leave it to that for the time being and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours instructed me to liaise with the Prosecution in relation to the upcoming visit of the experts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm allowed to make a record, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, let me be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A chance to get what your expert needed was missed, was lost, and this Chamber is quite convinced that it should do everything to assist the parties in getting what they need, and that's where we find ourselves at this moment. Let's leave it to that, and please -- but I see that Mr. File wants to make an observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Just a brief comment, Your Honour. I just wanted to emphasise for the clarity of the matter that there were not any meetings or communications between Defence and Prosecution about this issue once Ms. Radovanovic arrived and was working here during the week. I just wanted to make that clear. Also the one item that was skipped was the ICRC list. We did give Dr. Radovanovic the 2009 list, which is what Dr. Tabeau used in her report and which also encompasses the contents of the 2005 list. That also was not mentioned to us as an issue during that week. If it had been, that's the response we would have given them. And my final point was that I would have expected this also to be raised in the Defence 15th and 16th report on the Tomasica experts which was filed on the last day of Dr. Radovanovic's visit here. If there had been some issue for access, it could have been addressed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And the 2009 ICRC report is something we will discuss in due course, so we will have all that information. I just didn't want to be accused of testifying or influencing the witness in my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can -- I actually have to see if the -- where we left off. Okay. The question had been answered so we can move on to the next question. If we can turn to page 2 of the report in both languages, here you identify the engagement of your services and the assignment. Is what is written here in your report consistent with the mandate that you had in relation to this report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus for the next several questions on your visit to the ICTY premises in January of this year, and I'd first like to ask you to explain for us what was the purpose of that visit.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the visit was to check certain materials, that is to say, to have insight into materials used by Dr. Tabeau, particularly the internal database on mortality because I have never seen it. I do not know what it contains except that from some reports I could read what Dr. Tabeau says about it but not really in detail. It's rather superficial. So that was the basic purpose. I also wanted to receive reports or, rather, the materials that Dr. Tabeau mentions in her reports such as, for example, the certificates of death and so on, which she does not use -- or, rather, she uses them but which I haven't seen. I wished to see them here if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you perform the work while you were here at the ICTY individually or with the assistance of anyone?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I had the assistance of two assistants whom I financed personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how long did that site visit last?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 11th until the 17th of January, 2016.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time that you were at the ICTY Tribunal, were you permitted access to the actual Prosecution premises of the Demographic Unit or was your review conducted elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I conducted my work in the office of the Defence lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during your review of materials at The Hague in the Defence offices at the Tribunal, were you given full and unlimited access to the entirety of the Demographic Unit files and system or something else?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have unlimited access. I never, ever had it. What I got was something else; namely, what I asked for or, rather, one part of what I asked to inspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any access to the external sources cited by Dr. Tabeau, such as the ICMP database?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever seek directly from ICMP the material that had been sent to Dr. Tabeau as to Tomasica?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was the response of ICMP?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will paraphrase it briefly. The point was that I was to address the Prosecutor's office at ICTY because they had submitted it to the Prosecutor's office, and they said that they could not submit it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you given an ability to identify materials discovered during your stay at the ICTY as well as work product on the computers that you could ask to be copied and to receive later on to continue your work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received instructions to the effect that whatever I do, I may place in a specific file and take with me once it was time for me to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, one question. Did you ask the Prosecution for access to the ICMP database?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I addressed the ICMP directly and I did receive from the Prosecution the reports which Dr. Tabeau had received previously in the form of a table and a memo dating from June 2014. And I addressed ICMP at a later date, not I but the Defence, with a request stating exactly what I would like to receive from them, but they told me that they forwarded those materials to the Prosecution, but not proofs of death. They told me that they submitted that to the Prosecution also, but I haven't found them among the Prosecution materials. They then told me that I should address the Prosecutor's office of ICTY because they had recently submitted all those materials to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I received from Dr. Tabeau what she had received from ICMP. If that's all. I really don't know. I did receive some materials from her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that you were told that you could put documents in a file and that that would be copied and you could take it with you when you left. Were you able to get everything that you identified and put in that file folder to take with you? That is to say, was everything copied per your request?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not everything that I requested was copied. I requested -- I was looking for certain results that we concluded and also a mortality database because it includes a great number of files. So I wanted to take it with me because I could not inspect it completely in the short time that I spent here. The Prosecution responded by saying that I could not receive the internal mortality database but that they were forwarding me what was adequate to my needs and in accordance with the Rules. How the Prosecution knew what was adequate to my needs, I really don't know, and I also don't know what the Rules are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to be fair I will read into the record the e-mail which I received from the Office of the Prosecutor on this matter on the 26th of January, 2016. "Dear colleagues, we have completed our Rule 70 review of the material which your expert team had copied into the 'save' folder on your computers provided to them. On that basis, we have compiled a CD of files which we believe will satisfy the needs of your expert and our obligations. For instance, as you know, the large databases available here must remain on-site; in one case, where it appears that the expert team was seeking a large number of records associated with the 'Knjiga Nestalih Prijedor' within the integrated mortality database which we are unable to provide, we have instead provided both the 1998 and 2002 editions of the KNP to attempt to facilitate your expert's work. If there are additional types of material which your expert requires and we are unable to provide, please let us know, and we will work with you to provide relevant and non-privileged material. The complete CD will be placed in your locker today. Please do not hesitate to contact us with any questions." Now, let's talk about this integrated database of mortality. What was the purpose of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, how -- because I do understand that there's an unsatisfactory situation at this moment as far as disclosure is concerned, was a response sent to the Prosecution: This is not sufficient for us? Did you ask for any meeting to further discuss what was missing? Mr. Ivetic, could you clarify that issue for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After the visit of the experts to the ICTY, I don't -- I at least was not involved in any meetings with the Prosecution on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when did you receive -- or did you discuss this you just read from -- with the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the -- the -- the response of the Prosecution was indicated, and the expert indicated to me why they needed the integrated database which the Prosecution said they could not give to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you then or did the expert witness then contact the Prosecution to further discuss this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, let's talk about this integrated database of mortality. What was the purpose of you seeking that data source after the completion of your ICTY site visit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The integral database is a database consisting of ten other databases of which one deals with mortality. But Dr. Tabeau considers all these sources taken together the mortality database. I have never seen it. I saw it the first time in The Hague, and I tried during a short time to realise what it consists and what may be of assistance to me from this database. It has 56 characteristics listed in the heading, on the basis of which it may be concluded what Dr. Tabeau was doing, how she was doing the matching, what she considered good information, what she did not, and so on. It contains more than 181.000 lines but -- I call them "lines" but they relate to specific persons. What I could do over the few days that I was here was that it contained many double cases and to check how many of these there are. Dr. Tabeau notes that in some of her reports also and she says that such and such a portion are doubles. But even though I did not receive the criteria for matching, the later criteria as Dr. Tabeau calls them, as we will see later, I could not draw a conclusion what sort of combination was used. The fact that Prosecution offered me the book of the dead from Prijedor, it's a book that has been published and one can buy it. Why is this database secret? Of all the sources that it contains, most have been accessible to the public. Some of them I cannot reach, but as for the book of the missing, you can buy it. A lot of the information is published. There's the book of the dead published in Bosnia, including detailed information such as first and last name, the date of birth, and the date of death, and father's name, and so on. But I think that some information may be secret, such as autopsy reports and so on, but I also believe -- not that I believe, but that I'm signing a statement that I would keep a secret, and I'm fully grown up and I'm fully aware of the consequences that may follow if you violate such a statement. So I was really surprised when I learned that I could not take it with me. And I suppose that the only reason is that it contains particular details of certain individuals. For me, it's important because I could draw many characteristics from it and then formulate something precisely and in detail because Dr. Tabeau says that some information is detailed or matching. She shows how she matched certain information with the population census. I could also check how other sources of information match information, and for a certain time it would be sufficient for me to try to reach precise statistics that I would be willing to say with full accountability how reliable or unreliable it is. That was why I needed this database.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at P7449 in e-court, and I do have a paper copy in B/C/S for the witness since it is a long document. This will be Dr. Tabeau's report on Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the part I'd like to ask about is between pages 8 and 9 in the English under Part 2.7, and it is page 9 to 10 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I have received is my report and I -- if I understood you properly, you offered to provide me Dr. Tabeau's report. No, no, no. No. A mistake. I made a mistake only it's not the right page. I'm sorry. You said pages 9 and 10 in Serbian? That's why I thought it was not the same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be pages 9 and 10 in the Serbian, which is pages 8 to 9 in the English.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock and I see it's 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are starting to explore a new area, I think it would be better done after the break. Could the witness follow the usher. Ms. Radovanovic, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, we have before us Dr. Tabeau's report, P7449, and I believe we need the next page in the B/C/S. And once we get that, it should be, I believe, the second paragraph -- second full paragraph from the top in the B/C/S and it will be the bottom paragraph in the English that reads as follows: "In addition to the 1991 census, a number of victims were additionally searched for (if there was a need) in the integrated" --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I'm not able to follow. Let me know which page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is page 10 in the Serbian. It's on the screen right now. And it's the third paragraph from the top but it's the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll start again: "In addition to the 1991 census, a number of victims were additionally searched for (if this was a need) in the integrated BH mortality database (hereinafter: IntDB) developed in 2010, by the Demographic Unit of the OTP, which combines the information on war victims from numerous demographic sources on war mortality. The DU sources on war victims often contain information on detailed circumstances of death which may contribute to the proof that a certain victim was killed during the incident for which he was listed. The IntDB was only used" - if we can turn the English - "however, for double-checking information and not for extracting new one for the POD analysis in the present report." First off, Professor, is this integrated database that Dr. Tabeau is referencing in this part of her report the one that we have been talking that you sought access -- sought to take with you when you completed the site visit at the ICTY premises?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably. I didn't have the opportunity to see anything earlier or in another place to be able to make any kind of comparison. So I assume that that was the one that is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, in this part of her report, mentions that the database contains information on detailed circumstances of death. Were you able to find in the integrated database of mortality that was shown to you in January this type of detailed information on the circumstances of death that is described here?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the sources that I looked at, there are no detailed circumstances there. But, again, I have to say that I did that in five or six days, so I could not go through every source item by item, person by person. The database, in its heading, which was a main guide-line for me as to what I would look at, did not have a column on incidents that occurred for me to be able to say, well, I'm going to follow that particular column in order to see what the source of the data was. The sources that I've looked at, and I looked at all of them other than the registrar of births for Mostar, which I assume would not relate to Prijedor, contained documents from where I could see what the incidents were in which the victims were killed. There is something that the B and H prosecutor's office submitted to Dr. Tabeau but that was in the internal database. I received that separately. There are some documents but these were not persons that were already identified. These were persons that were going to be identified on the basis of the DNA analysis, and they were descriptions, some there, as to incidents that happened, and there is a number of reports about identification of mortal remains where there were some details about it or not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor -- Professor, the translators have asked that you please slow down in giving your answers so that they can properly transmit everything that you say to those that are following the English channel. So if I could ask you to please slow down. And it appears that we lost what you were saying immediately after you started to say: "... as to incidents that happened, and there is a number of reports about identification of mortal remains where there was some details about it or not," and that's where the translators lost you. So if you could please take up your answer from that point.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are some reports received from the B and H prosecutor's offices. These are reports establishing the identity where in some of them you can actually see the circumstances in which somebody died. There are also reports where persons are listed that had not yet been identified on the basis of DNA analysis, and there are some details about how those victims died. One can draw some conclusions on the basis of this information about how those persons died. But at that time, that was not in the database. I don't know whether Dr. Tabeau is going to add that or not. I received a certain number of material which does not overlap with the number of victims that were given by Dr. Tabeau and that does not overlap with the information that she received from the BiH prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just so we can be clear, these records or reports that were received from the B and H prosecutor's office, were such types of materials within the integrated mortality database or not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I received them separately. I don't know whether they are a part of it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you, I think, earlier identified ten sources that were in the integrated mortality database. Do you recall what those sources were? You've mentioned the Mostar books of dead. What were the other sources?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were the Red Cross lists from 2009. There was the Prijedor book of the dead. Then the DEM-2T database which includes all of the soldiers. Then there was a separate database about soldiers of the Republika Srpska and about Croat soldiers. Then was information about exhumations. Then there was information from the Muslims Against Genocide organisation. I think I have listed all the sources. I'm not quite sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to read to you something that Dr. Tabeau has testified about during her testimony at our trial last year as to Tomasica and then I will have some questions for you. This was from transcript page 36716, line 18, through 36717, line 10: "The reference sources shown on this slide are the 1991 population census for Bosnia-Herzegovina and the integrated mortality database, which is an integration of a large number of sources on both known deaths and missing persons, again, for Bosnia and Herzegovina, entire country. These sources are part of the usual methodology that my unit and myself have been using in compiling our reports. So the methodology involves linking a list of victims, say, Tomasica identified persons, back with the 1991 population census to confirm their personal details and whereabouts at the outbreak of the war, like place of residence and to study the ethnicity, et cetera. And the integrated database is a list of victims that have been also exposed additionally to checks in the sources on survivors, like records of internally displaced persons, refugees and voters registered for 1997, 1998, and 2000 elections in Bosnia, country-wide elections in Bosnia. This is to exclude potential survivors or actual real survivors who should not appear on the lists of victims. So it is -- this reference sources are part of the usual proof of death routine of my unit and myself. So the abbreviation POD on this slide stands for the proof of death review routine." Professor, did you have occasion to discover what methodology of matching Dr. Tabeau utilized for her integrated database of mortality that she describes here is part of the usual routine of her unit and herself?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that it was part of the usual routine, but this is not how it is done in scientific studies. Based on what I could see in the internal database, I could see what Dr. Tabeau marked in that database as matched. It's under the item "match." And that's why it would have been important to me, in view of the rules that she used, to take it and to actually study that particular database in detail. Dr. Tabeau also says there that these are usual sources of data that her team uses but does not say that these are usual sources of data that are used in scientifically based statistical demographic research, and this is a crucial difference. And if you permit me to ask for a piece of paper, since it's quite a long quotation, I would need to take some notes. I don't know if I'm allowed to make the notes on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Professor. I have some blank paper here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're at it, I'd ask for 1D6189 of which I have a hard copy, since I know the professor likes to use her magnifying-glass to read things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would ask for 1D6189 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now while we have both versions on the screen, Professor, could you explain for us what this is that we are looking at. Where did this come from?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that I did here in The Hague. I took out this as examples. There was around a hundred of such examples, but as they were very similar I believed it was sufficient for me to present these. It's a comparison and this comes from the internal database on mortality. Comparison of information received from ICRC and the population census. The last column, matched, marked with 1, which means that there is a correspondence of information. I can now read first and last names, but let me not do that. I will just draw your attention to the ICRC list where the person with this first and last name, and father's name as well, born on 6th of May, 1973, in Prijedor, that is the place of birth, and that's the information from the ICRC. Matched with the population census, a person with the first -- with the same first name, last name, and father's name but born six years later, not on the same date, not on the same day, and in a different place, and Dr. Tabeau says that she matched this. I suppose -- or, rather, I don't suppose, but if the first and last names are identical, and we know that in the census there have been many corrections, I really don't know how many and how, and I don't know if this was done in ICRC as well in terms of first and last names but it probably was, then matching on the basis that persons have identical name only when you have the information that such a person was born in a different place at a different date with a difference of six years and you say you've matched this person with the census, this is something that I, as an expert who deals with this sort of things, would really question. And all the examples are similar, if you want me to read them, but more or less, it's about the dates and places which differ. The only thing that is identical in all examples are the first and last names and the father's name. Let me repeat that as early as in 2005, when asking how many corrections were made to the census, as I note in my report on Srebrenica, I requested from the demographic department and Dr. Tabeau to tell me how many corrections and how many visual assessments that they were matched was done, I received an answer that there were thousands of names that were corrected and that probably there were as many visual assessments that they were matched.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question, perhaps a matter of detail, but could you look at the fourth name listed here. Because you explained to us this was all persons with the same family name, same first name, and same father's name. Now I see that the father's name is not the same on this fourth entry. Is there -- in view of what you -- if view of what told us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have seen it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that a mistake or is it that you made a mistake when you said that these names are all the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a mistake, but I think that I said mostly all names are the same. We can go through them one item after another, but this is absolutely taken out from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's no need to do that. I understood that you said all names are the same, but I leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you could clarify for us this column that says "matched" and has a number 1 which you said there was correspondence of identity, who -- who or whom has matched the two columns or the two -- the two -- the two names to say it's the same person? Was that something that you did?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is information taken from the internal mortality database, and if you see the source is noted at the bottom of the table. I only looked and reviewed the database, and I am not supposed to correct or add or take out anything from or to that database.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said generally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, what does 5 under the column "new ethnicity" signify; and what does 1 under "matched" signify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 1 signifies that the match is accepted, that it's been matched. Number 0 stands for no match. And if there is a match, it means there is a correspondence. And number 5 is a designation for ethnicity taken over from the population census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And which ethnicity is number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated that generally the matching appears to be related to the name, last name, and father's name. How reliable is that type of matching, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's very little reliability. Even though in reports on Srebrenica, Dr. Tabeau and Dr. Brunborg claim that in a small area such as Srebrenica the likelihood that somebody has the same first and last name is very small. The ARK later represented by Dr. Tabeau and Prijedor, which in 1991 had more than 100.000 inhabitants, I believe, may happen to have persons with the same first and last names. Though I haven't checked that. But my deep conviction and on the basis of my experience with previous matchings, I know that some names were corrected, and whether they are present as such in the ICRC database or whether there was a mistake and then it was corrected in the census, I really don't know. I can just tell you as a curiosity that in the census in Bosnia-Herzegovina there are five persons with the name Svetlana Radovanovic, with the identical first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Judge Moloto asked you about the number 5 under the column "new ethnicity." What is the meaning of the column --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is the meaning of the column "new ethnicity"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I know for sure, in the population census, the response on ethnicity is collected and then entered in letters, but when the census is processed, then there are codes. So the material is first encoded and it's called a codex of ethnicity in which each ethnicity has been designated a specific number so that, for example, a Serb is number 7, the Muslim 5, the Croat -- I can't remember all of the ethnicities, but the codex included 20-odd nationalities in the 1991 population census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said in the Bosnia-Herzegovina census, you found five names by Svetlana Radovanovic. Was the father's name also the same for all five?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems you haven't understood me well. I didn't say Muslims, but there are five Svetlana Radovanovics and I am an a citizen of Serbia, so I looked for the first and last name. Even if there is no father's name, if you try to do the matching on the basis of 72 criteria, as Dr. Tabeau says, someplace she would use the initial. So I -- I didn't mean matching with Muslims but matching with the census of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The total population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm also not asking you about Muslims. I don't know where you get Muslims from. You said that you looked at the Bosnia-Herzegovina census list and you saw five Svetlana Radovanovics. You're trying to show that going by the name and last name is not a safe way of identifying people. What we have been talking about here, you have been criticising not just the name -- first name and last name, but first name, last name, and father's name. Hence I'm asking you: Do the five Svetlana Radovanovics that you have found, do they have the same name of the father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they don't have the same father's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That was all my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I think the confusion lies in the transcript having the word "Muslim" inserted and I think that's what the translation to the witness was in your question so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there was any confusion in that respect, then it has now been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're at the time for the break, Your Honours. I would just tender this document at this time and then we can take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D6189 will be Exhibit D1464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Professor Radovanovic, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, and I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given, and that includes any evidence you have given earlier, or evidence still to be given. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 26th of April, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of April, 2016, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
